tool.name: asyncio
tool.tagline: Python's built-in framework for concurrent I/O with async and await
tool.description: asyncio is the standard library's event loop and toolkit for writing concurrent code with async/await. It lets one thread juggle thousands of network connections, API calls or subprocesses, and it underpins async web frameworks such as FastAPI, aiohttp and many database drivers. Learn it to write fast I/O-bound programs and to understand what async libraries do under the hood.

glossary.def: Anything you can put after await in Python: a coroutine, a Task or a Future.
In Python, a function defined with async def (a coroutine function). Calling it gives a coroutine, which runs when you await it.
Sharing one thread by taking turns: each piece of code runs until it chooses to pause and hand over, and nothing is interrupted in the middle.
An asyncio object that wraps a coroutine and hands it to the event loop, so it runs alongside other code. Await the task to get its result.
An object standing for a result that isn't ready yet. Code can await it; something else fills in the result later.
Asking a running asyncio task to stop early. A CancelledError is raised inside it at the await where it is paused, so its clean-up code still runs.
An asyncio tool used with async with: it starts related tasks, waits for all of them when the block ends, and cancels the rest if one fails.
A rule that tasks running at the same time live inside one clearly marked block of code and are all finished when it ends, so none are left running or forgotten.
A Python exception that bundles several exceptions together, for example from several tasks that failed at once; handled with except*.
The exception asyncio raises inside a task to cancel it. Let it pass through: if you catch it, raise it again.
A lock with a fixed number of keys: at most that many pieces of code can hold it at once, and the rest wait. Used to limit how many things run at the same time.
A function defined with async def that contains yield. It hands out values one at a time and may await between them; loop over it with async for.
An object you loop over with async for; getting each next item may involve waiting, for example for data from the network.
An object used with async with whose setup and clean-up steps may await, such as opening and closing a network connection.
The asyncio object you read incoming bytes from on a network connection, for example line by line with readline().
The asyncio object you write bytes to on a network connection; await its drain() after writing to wait until the data has gone out.
End of file: the sign that there is no more data to read, because a file ended or the other side closed the connection.
asyncio's lower-level networking layer: a transport sends and receives the bytes, and a protocol object's methods are called back when data arrives.
An operating-system feature (epoll, kqueue or IOCP) that watches many connections at once and reports which ones are ready to read or write.
When one piece of work runs so long without pausing that other work waiting for its turn is badly delayed.
An asyncio setting that adds extra checks and warnings, such as reporting slow steps and coroutines that were never awaited.
An asyncio task that starts running immediately when it is created, instead of waiting for its turn on the event loop; if it finishes without pausing, it is never scheduled at all.
A third-party replacement for asyncio's event loop, written in C, that often makes network-heavy Python programs faster.

concepts.name: Coroutines and asyncio.run
concepts.summary: Write functions that can pause while they wait, with async def and await, and start them with asyncio.run().
concepts.why: Every asyncio program starts here: nothing async runs until asyncio.run() starts it and await drives it.
concepts.body:
Much of what programs do is wait: for a web page to download, a database to answer, a big file to load. Reading or writing data outside the program like this is called **I/O** (input/output). While ordinary Python code waits for one download, it does nothing else.

Making progress on several jobs during the same stretch of time, switching to another whenever one is waiting, is **concurrency**. Think of a cook who chops vegetables while the kettle boils instead of staring at the kettle. Code that starts a slow job and carries on with other work meanwhile is called **asynchronous**, or async for short. asyncio is the part of the standard library that does this.

A function defined with `async def` is a **coroutine function**. Calling it does not run its body. Much like a generator function, it gives back an object, here a **coroutine**: a function call that can pause in the middle and resume later.

Something has to run coroutines and decide which one goes next. That's the **event loop**, the part of asyncio that decides what runs next. `asyncio.run(main())` creates an event loop, runs the coroutine `main()` to the end, closes the loop and returns the result. Call it once, at the top of your program.

Inside a coroutine, `await` runs something and gives you its result. Anything you can await is an **awaitable**; coroutines are the first kind you'll meet. While the awaited thing waits (a timer, a download), your coroutine pauses and hands control back to the event loop, which can run other coroutines meanwhile. That's the whole trick: coroutines take turns, pausing at each `await`, all inside one program.

- `await` only works inside `async def` (or in the asyncio REPL, `python -m asyncio`).
- Calling a coroutine function without `await` creates a coroutine that never runs, and Python warns "coroutine ... was never awaited".

An `async def` function can call normal functions freely, but a normal function cannot `await`. That's why an asyncio program has one `asyncio.run()` at the top and `async def` functions all the way down from there.
concepts.code:
import asyncio

async def greet(name: str) -> str:
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)          # pause here; other coroutines could run
    return f"hello, {name}"

async def main() -> None:
    coro = greet("ada")
    print(type(coro).__name__)        # coroutine  (nothing has run yet)
    print(await coro)                 # hello, ada

result = asyncio.run(main())
print(result)                         # None  (main returns nothing)
takeaways: Calling an async def function only creates a coroutine object
await runs an awaitable and lets other coroutines run while it waits
asyncio.run() starts the event loop; call it once at the top
pitfalls: Forgetting await: the coroutine never runs and you get a RuntimeWarning instead of a result.

quiz.q: What does calling an async def function, f(), return without await?
options: A coroutine object that has not started
quiz.explain: Calling a coroutine function only builds the coroutine; it runs when awaited or scheduled.

concepts.name: Concurrency vs blocking
concepts.summary: See why asyncio.sleep lets other coroutines run while time.sleep freezes the whole event loop.
concepts.why: Putting calls that freeze the program into async code is the most common reason asyncio programs are slow.
concepts.body:
asyncio runs all coroutines on one **thread**: a single line of work that the computer carries out one step at a time. The coroutines take turns, and a coroutine only gives up its turn at an `await` that actually waits.

This is **cooperative multitasking**. It's like people sharing one microphone: nobody grabs it, each speaker hands it over voluntarily when they pause.

`await asyncio.sleep(1)` tells the event loop "wake me in a second" and gives up the turn at once, so other coroutines run in the meantime. `time.sleep(1)` is an ordinary **blocking** call: it makes the whole thread stop and wait, doing nothing else. With it stop the event loop and every other coroutine.

Ordinary code like that, which does one thing at a time and waits for each step to finish, is called **synchronous** (sync). Any slow sync call inside a coroutine blocks in the same way:

- `requests.get(...)` from the popular `requests` library, or a sync library for a database,
- `open().read()` on a slow disk,
- long calculations, such as checking millions of numbers or processing a huge file.

All of these stall the loop. Use libraries written for asyncio instead (aiohttp or httpx to download web pages, asyncpg for the PostgreSQL database), or hand the blocking call to a separate thread with `asyncio.to_thread`, which you'll meet later.

The example runs three one-second waits concurrently with `asyncio.gather` (explained two lessons on), finishing in about one second in total. With `time.sleep` it takes three seconds, even though the code looks the same. `await asyncio.sleep(0)` is a handy trick: it gives up the turn once without waiting, letting other ready coroutines run.
concepts.code:
import asyncio, time

async def wait_async(n):
    await asyncio.sleep(1)            # gives the turn back to the loop
    return n

async def wait_blocking(n):
    time.sleep(1)                     # freezes the whole thread
    return n

async def timed(fn):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    res = await asyncio.gather(fn(1), fn(2), fn(3))   # run all three
    print(fn.__name__, res, f"{time.perf_counter() - t:.1f}s")

asyncio.run(timed(wait_async))        # wait_async [1, 2, 3] 1.0s
asyncio.run(timed(wait_blocking))     # wait_blocking [1, 2, 3] 3.0s
takeaways: Coroutines only switch at await points that really wait
Blocking calls (time.sleep, requests, long calculations) freeze every coroutine
Use async libraries or asyncio.to_thread for blocking work
pitfalls: Calling a sync library such as requests inside async def and wondering why nothing runs at the same time.

quiz.q: Three coroutines each call time.sleep(1) and are run with gather. Roughly how long does it take?
quiz.explain: time.sleep freezes the one thread the event loop runs on, so the sleeps happen one after another.

concepts.name: Tasks: running coroutines concurrently
concepts.summary: Wrap coroutines in Tasks with asyncio.create_task so they run in the background while you do other work.
concepts.why: Awaiting coroutines one by one runs them sequentially; Tasks are how you actually get concurrency.
concepts.body:
`await coro()` runs a coroutine and waits for it right there. Two awaits one after another run one after the other. To run things at the same time, schedule them as **Tasks**.

`task = asyncio.create_task(coro())` wraps the coroutine in a Task and hands it to the event loop. The loop starts running it the next time the current coroutine pauses at an `await`. Meanwhile you can do other work, and later `await task` to get its result (or the exception it raised).

A Task is a kind of **Future**: an object standing for a result that isn't ready yet, like a ticket you exchange for your order when it's done. Useful Task methods:

- `task.done()`, `task.result()`, `task.exception()`,
- `task.cancel()` asks the task to stop early, which is called **cancellation** (more on it later),
- `task.add_done_callback(fn)`, `task.get_name()`.

One rule matters a lot: **keep a reference** to tasks you create. Python deletes objects that nothing refers to, and the event loop's own hold on a task doesn't count. So a "fire-and-forget" task stored nowhere can vanish in the middle of running. Store tasks in a variable or a set, or better, use a TaskGroup (a later lesson), which keeps its tasks for you.

Also make sure every task is eventually awaited. If a task fails and nobody awaits it, its exception is only printed as a warning, "Task exception was never retrieved", when the task is deleted, which is easy to miss.
concepts.code:
import asyncio, time

async def fetch(name, delay):
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)            # stands in for a download
    return f"{name} done"

async def main():
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    a = asyncio.create_task(fetch("a", 1.0))
    b = asyncio.create_task(fetch("b", 1.0))
    print(a.done())                       # False: scheduled, not finished
    print(await a, await b)               # a done b done
    print(f"{time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f}s")  # 1.0s, not 2.0s

asyncio.run(main())
takeaways: create_task schedules a coroutine to run concurrently
Await the task later to get its result or exception
Keep a reference to every task you create
pitfalls: Creating a task and not storing it anywhere; it may be deleted mid-run or its error silently lost.

quiz.q: Why does a program that awaits fetch('a') then fetch('b') take twice as long as one using create_task?
options: Sequential awaits wait for the first to finish before starting the second
quiz.explain: Plain awaits run in order; tasks are scheduled up front so their waits overlap.

concepts.name: Waiting for many: gather
concepts.summary: Run several awaitables concurrently and collect their results in order with asyncio.gather.
concepts.why: Starting many downloads or lookups at once and collecting the answers is the bread-and-butter asyncio pattern.
concepts.body:
`await asyncio.gather(a(), b(), c())` turns each awaitable into a task, waits for all of them, and returns a list of results **in the order you passed them**, not the order they finished. To pass a whole series, put a star in front of a generator expression: `await asyncio.gather(*(fetch(u) for u in urls))`.

Error handling is the part to understand:

- By default, the first exception raised by any of them comes straight out of `gather`. The other tasks are **not cancelled**; they keep running in the background.
- With `return_exceptions=True`, exceptions are put in the result list in place of values, so you can inspect every outcome.

If you want "fail fast and cancel the rest", use `asyncio.TaskGroup` (Python 3.11+, a later lesson), now the recommended way to run a group of related tasks. `gather` remains handy for quick jobs, for collecting each item's failure with `return_exceptions=True`, and in code that must support older Python versions.

When you start hundreds of jobs, limit how many run at once (for example with a semaphore, covered later), so you don't open 10,000 network connections at the same moment.
concepts.code:
import asyncio

async def square(n):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1 * (5 - n))    # later items finish first
    if n == 3:
        raise ValueError("bad 3")
    return n * n

async def main():
    ok = await asyncio.gather(square(1), square(2))
    print(ok)                             # [1, 4]  (argument order)
    res = await asyncio.gather(*(square(n) for n in range(1, 5)),
                               return_exceptions=True)
    print(res)                            # [1, 4, ValueError('bad 3'), 16]
    try:
        await asyncio.gather(square(3), square(4))
    except ValueError as e:
        print("raised:", e)               # raised: bad 3

asyncio.run(main())
takeaways: gather returns results in argument order
The first error is raised to you, but the other tasks keep running
return_exceptions=True puts exceptions into the results list
pitfalls: Assuming gather cancels the other tasks when one fails; it doesn't.

quiz.q: gather(a(), b()) where b raises first. What happens to a?
options: Its result is returned with the error
It keeps running in the background
quiz.explain: gather passes the first exception on to you but does not cancel the remaining tasks.

concepts.name: Timeouts
concepts.summary: Put a time limit on how long an operation may take, with asyncio.timeout() or asyncio.wait_for().
concepts.why: A download or a reply from another computer can hang forever; real programs limit how long they wait.
concepts.body:
A **timeout** is a limit on how long you're willing to wait before giving up with an error, like hanging up when nobody answers the phone after a minute.

Since Python 3.11, the preferred tool is `asyncio.timeout(delay)`, used with `async with`, the async version of the `with` statement you know from files. Everything inside the block must finish within `delay` seconds. If it doesn't, the current task is cancelled at the `await` where it's waiting. On leaving the block, that cancellation is turned into a `TimeoutError`, a built-in exception (`asyncio.TimeoutError` is another name for it).

```python
async with asyncio.timeout(2):
    data = await fetch()
```

The block can contain several awaits, and they share one deadline. `asyncio.timeout_at(when)` takes the deadline as a moment on the event loop's own clock (`loop.time()`) instead of a number of seconds, and the object it returns has `reschedule()` to move the deadline. Pass `None` for no limit.

`asyncio.wait_for(aw, timeout)` is the older form for a single awaitable; since 3.12 it is built on `timeout()`. It cancels the awaitable when time runs out and raises `TimeoutError`.

When the work is cancelled, its `finally` blocks still run, so clean-up happens. Catch `TimeoutError` outside the `async with` block, not inside it: inside the block, the cancellation hasn't been turned into `TimeoutError` yet.
concepts.code:
import asyncio

async def slow():
    try:
        await asyncio.sleep(10)
    finally:
        print("slow: cleaning up")        # runs when cancelled too

async def main():
    try:
        async with asyncio.timeout(0.2):
            await slow()
    except TimeoutError:
        print("timed out")
    # sleep(0.01, "fast") waits, then returns "fast"
    print(await asyncio.wait_for(asyncio.sleep(0.01, "fast"), timeout=1))

asyncio.run(main())
# slow: cleaning up
# timed out
# fast
takeaways: async with asyncio.timeout(s): sets one deadline for a block
On expiry the work is cancelled and TimeoutError is raised
wait_for(aw, timeout) is the single-awaitable form
pitfalls: Catching TimeoutError inside the timeout block; catch it around the async with.

quiz.q: What exception do you catch after an asyncio.timeout(1) block expires (Python 3.11+)?
options: Nothing is raised; it returns None
quiz.explain: The cancellation is converted to the built-in TimeoutError when the block exits.

concepts.name: TaskGroup and structured concurrency
concepts.summary: Use asyncio.TaskGroup to start related tasks that are always awaited together and cancelled together on failure.
concepts.why: TaskGroup removes leaked tasks and lost errors, the two classic asyncio bugs.
concepts.body:
`asyncio.TaskGroup` (3.11+) gives you **structured concurrency**: tasks started in a group cannot outlive the `async with` block that owns them, the way a function's local variables can't outlive the function.

```python
async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
    t1 = tg.create_task(fetch(1))
    t2 = tg.create_task(fetch(2))
# here both are finished
```

Leaving the block waits for all tasks. If any task raises, the group cancels the remaining tasks, waits for them to finish, and then raises an **ExceptionGroup**, a single exception that holds every error that wasn't a cancellation. Handle it with `except*`, which picks out the exceptions inside the group by type:

```python
except* ValueError as eg:
    for e in eg.exceptions: ...
```

Compared with `gather`, a TaskGroup never leaves tasks running after a failure, keeps its own references to its tasks so none vanish, and reports all errors, not just the first. It is the right default for "do these N things concurrently".

Read results from the task objects after the block: `t1.result()`. To limit how many run at once inside a group, combine it with a semaphore. To end a group early on purpose, the 3.13 docs suggest raising your own exception class from a task and catching it with `except*` outside the block.
concepts.code:
import asyncio

async def work(n):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1 * n)
    if n == 2:
        raise ValueError(f"task {n} failed")
    print(f"task {n} finished")
    return n

async def main():
    try:
        async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
            tasks = [tg.create_task(work(n)) for n in (1, 2, 3)]
    except* ValueError as eg:
        print("errors:", [str(e) for e in eg.exceptions])
    print([t.cancelled() for t in tasks])

asyncio.run(main())
# task 1 finished
# errors: ['task 2 failed']
# [False, False, True]   (task 3 was cancelled)
takeaways: Tasks in a TaskGroup are all done when the async with block exits
One failure cancels the other tasks in the group
Errors arrive as an ExceptionGroup; handle with except*
pitfalls: Using plain except ValueError around a TaskGroup; the group raises ExceptionGroup, so use except*.

quiz.q: In a TaskGroup, task A raises while B is still sleeping. What happens to B?
options: It keeps running after the block exits
The ExceptionGroup is raised immediately without waiting for B
It is cancelled and awaited before the block exits
quiz.explain: The group cancels remaining tasks and waits for them before raising the ExceptionGroup.

concepts.name: Cancellation and cleanup
concepts.summary: Cancel tasks with task.cancel(), clean up with try/finally, and know when to re-raise CancelledError.
concepts.why: Timeouts, TaskGroups and shutting a program down cleanly all work through cancellation, so your code must cooperate with it.
concepts.body:
`task.cancel()` asks a task to stop. The next time the task is paused at an `await`, a `CancelledError` exception is raised inside it, right at that `await`. The exception travels up through the coroutine like any other, running `finally` blocks and `async with` exits on the way, so resources get released.

Rules for code that cancels cleanly:

- Put clean-up in `finally` or a context manager. Clean-up may itself `await` (closing a network connection, for example).
- If you catch `CancelledError` to log or tidy up, **re-raise it** with a bare `raise`. Swallowing it breaks `asyncio.timeout()`, TaskGroup and the shutdown done by `asyncio.run()`, which all rely on the cancellation finishing.
- `CancelledError` is a subclass of `BaseException`, not `Exception`, so `except Exception` does not catch it. That's deliberate.

After a task is cancelled, `task.cancelled()` is True and awaiting it raises `CancelledError`. `cancel("reason")` attaches a message.

`asyncio.shield(aw)` protects an inner awaitable when the outer one is cancelled. The outer `await` still raises `CancelledError`, but the shielded work keeps running. That's useful for work that must not stop halfway, such as finishing writing a file or saving a payment. Keep a reference to the shielded task so it isn't lost.

Cancellation only lands at an `await`: a long calculation with no awaits cannot be cancelled until it reaches one.
concepts.code:
import asyncio

async def worker():
    try:
        while True:
            await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        print("worker: cancelled, closing")
        raise                              # always re-raise
    finally:
        print("worker: finally ran")

async def main():
    t = asyncio.create_task(worker())
    await asyncio.sleep(0.25)
    t.cancel("shutting down")
    try:
        await t
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        print("main: cancelled() =", t.cancelled())

asyncio.run(main())
# worker: cancelled, closing
# worker: finally ran
# main: cancelled() = True
takeaways: cancel() raises CancelledError inside the task at its next await
Clean up in finally / async with; re-raise CancelledError if you catch it
shield() protects an inner operation from outer cancellation
pitfalls: Wrapping a loop body in except BaseException (or except CancelledError) without re-raising, making the task uncancellable.

quiz.q: Why does except Exception not catch asyncio.CancelledError?
options: It is a subclass of BaseException, not Exception
Cancellation is not an exception at all
asyncio suppresses it before your code sees it
quiz.explain: Since 3.8 CancelledError inherits from BaseException so generic handlers don't swallow it.

concepts.name: Producer-consumer with asyncio.Queue
concepts.summary: Pass work between coroutines with asyncio.Queue, using a fixed set of worker tasks.
concepts.why: Queues limit how much runs at once and slow down a fast producer, for crawlers, pipelines and job runners.
concepts.body:
`asyncio.Queue` is a line of items for coroutines: first in, first out, like the line at a checkout. (It's for coroutines sharing one thread; code using several threads needs `queue.Queue` instead.) `await q.put(item)` waits if the queue is full (when created with `maxsize`), and `await q.get()` waits until an item is available.

That waiting gives **backpressure**: the code putting items in (the producer) automatically slows down to match the code taking them out (the consumers), so items never pile up without limit.

The standard pattern is a fixed set of **workers**, tasks that each repeatedly take a job and do it:

- start N workers that loop: `item = await q.get()`, handle the item, `q.task_done()`,
- the producer puts items,
- `await q.join()` waits until every item put has been marked done.

Then the workers must be stopped. Before 3.13 you cancelled them, or put one special "stop" value in the queue per worker. **Python 3.13 adds `q.shutdown()`**: after it, `put()` raises `QueueShutDown`, and `get()` raises `QueueShutDown` once the queue is empty, so workers can leave their loop cleanly. `shutdown(immediate=True)` also throws away items still waiting.

`PriorityQueue` (smallest item first) and `LifoQueue` (last in, first out) are variants. Use the `_nowait` methods (`put_nowait`, `get_nowait`) when you must not wait, and handle `QueueFull` / `QueueEmpty`.

The number of workers is your limit on how much runs at once, which is often clearer than a semaphore (next lesson).
concepts.code:
import asyncio

async def worker(name, q, results):
    while True:
        try:
            n = await q.get()
        except asyncio.QueueShutDown:      # 3.13+
            return
        await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
        results.append(n * n)
        q.task_done()

async def main():
    q, results = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=3), []
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        for i in range(2):
            tg.create_task(worker(f"w{i}", q, results))
        for n in range(6):
            await q.put(n)                 # waits while the queue is full
        await q.join()                     # all items processed
        q.shutdown()                       # workers exit their loops
    print(sorted(results))                 # [0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25]

asyncio.run(main())
takeaways: put() waits when full, get() waits when empty: built-in backpressure
Pair every get() with task_done() so join() can finish
3.13's Queue.shutdown() stops workers without special stop values
pitfalls: Forgetting task_done(), so await q.join() hangs forever.

quiz.q: What does await q.join() wait for?
options: task_done() to be called for every item that was put
The next item to be put
quiz.explain: join() tracks unfinished items; each put increments the count and each task_done() decrements it.

concepts.name: Locks, semaphores and events
concepts.summary: Coordinate coroutines with asyncio.Lock, Semaphore and Event.
concepts.why: Data that several coroutines change, and limits on how many calls run at once, still need coordination, even on one thread.
concepts.body:
Coroutines run on one thread, so a single statement like `x += 1` can't be interrupted. But any sequence that **awaits in the middle** can: read a value, await something, write it back, and another coroutine may have changed the value in between. A bug like that, where the result depends on which code happens to run first, is a **race condition**.

asyncio provides coordination tools for coroutines (the versions for threads live in the `threading` module):

- `asyncio.Lock`: `async with lock:` lets only one coroutine inside the block at a time; the others wait their turn.
- `asyncio.Semaphore(n)`: a **semaphore** is a lock with n keys, so at most n coroutines are inside at once. It's the standard way to cap how many calls you make to a service at the same time. `BoundedSemaphore` raises an error if it's released more times than acquired.
- `asyncio.Event`: one coroutine calls `event.set()`, and every coroutine paused on `await event.wait()` wakes up. Good for "ready" or "shutdown" signals.
- `asyncio.Condition` and `asyncio.Barrier` (3.11) cover rarer cases.

Each of these attaches itself to the event loop that is running when it's first used. So create them inside async code, or at least never share one between separate `asyncio.run()` calls.

A semaphore around many tasks is the simplest way to limit how many calls run at once: start all the tasks with `gather`, and have each one enter the semaphore before its call.
concepts.code:
import asyncio

sem, active, peak = asyncio.Semaphore(2), [], 0

async def call_api(i):
    global peak
    async with sem:                      # at most 2 inside at once
        active.append(i); peak = max(peak, len(active))
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
        active.remove(i)
    return i

async def main():
    ready = asyncio.Event()
    async def waiter():
        await ready.wait()
        print("waiter: go!")
    w = asyncio.create_task(waiter())
    print(await asyncio.gather(*(call_api(i) for i in range(6))))
    ready.set(); await w
    print("peak concurrency:", peak)

asyncio.run(main())
# [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5] / waiter: go! / peak concurrency: 2
takeaways: Race conditions can happen across await points, even on one thread
Semaphore(n) caps how many operations run at once
Event sends a one-time signal to many waiters
pitfalls: Using threading.Lock in async code: waiting for it blocks the whole event loop.

quiz.q: Which tool is the usual way to allow at most 10 downloads running at the same time?
quiz.explain: A semaphore with 10 keys lets up to 10 coroutines inside at once; the rest wait.

concepts.name: Running blocking code: to_thread
concepts.summary: Hand blocking or older sync calls to threads with asyncio.to_thread, or to processes with run_in_executor.
concepts.why: Real programs use sync libraries too; handing their calls to threads keeps the event loop responsive.
concepts.body:
Sometimes async code must call something that blocks: a sync library for some company's service, reading a big file, `time.sleep`. Called directly, it stalls every coroutine. Instead:

`result = await asyncio.to_thread(func, *args, **kwargs)` runs `func` in a separate thread and awaits its result. The thread comes from the loop's default **thread pool**: a `ThreadPoolExecutor`, the executor you met in the threads lesson, which keeps a few threads ready for jobs. Because a thread waiting on I/O lets go of the GIL, many such calls can overlap.

For **CPU-bound** code (long calculations that keep the processor busy), threads don't help on a standard Python build, because of the GIL. Use a process pool:

```python
loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
with ProcessPoolExecutor() as pool:
    r = await loop.run_in_executor(pool, cpu_heavy, data)
```

`run_in_executor(None, func, *args)` uses the default thread pool and passes only positional arguments; for keyword arguments, wrap the call as `functools.partial(func, key=value)`.

The opposite direction, running async code from another thread, uses `asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(coro, loop)`, which returns a `concurrent.futures.Future`, or `loop.call_soon_threadsafe(cb)` for a plain callback. Never touch the event loop from another thread without these.

The default thread pool has a limited number of threads (`min(32, os.process_cpu_count() + 4)` in 3.13), so thousands of slow blocking calls will wait in line; at that scale, find an async library.
concepts.code:
import asyncio, time

def blocking_io(n):
    time.sleep(0.5)                     # a sync library call
    return n * 10

async def heartbeat():
    for _ in range(3):
        print("tick")
        await asyncio.sleep(0.2)

async def main():
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    results = await asyncio.gather(
        asyncio.to_thread(blocking_io, 1),
        asyncio.to_thread(blocking_io, 2),
        heartbeat(),                    # keeps ticking meanwhile
    )
    print(results[:2], f"{time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f}s")

asyncio.run(main())
# tick / tick / tick, then: [10, 20] 0.6s
takeaways: asyncio.to_thread(func, ...) awaits a blocking call without freezing the loop
Use run_in_executor with a ProcessPoolExecutor for CPU-bound work
run_coroutine_threadsafe hands a coroutine to the loop from another thread
pitfalls: Using to_thread for heavy pure-Python calculations and expecting a speedup on a standard (GIL) build.

quiz.q: A sync library call takes 2 s and blocks. How do you call it from a coroutine without freezing other tasks?
quiz.explain: to_thread runs it in a separate thread and gives you an awaitable; the other options need a coroutine.

concepts.name: Processing results as they finish
concepts.summary: Handle results in completion order with asyncio.as_completed, or wait for the first one with asyncio.wait.
concepts.why: Showing the fastest answer first, or asking several copies of a service and using whichever replies first, needs completion order rather than argument order.
concepts.body:
`gather` gives you results in argument order only after everything finishes. Often you want each result as soon as it is ready.

`asyncio.as_completed(aws)` yields results in completion order. In **Python 3.13 you can also loop over it with `async for`, and it then gives you the original tasks**, which makes it easy to know which input finished:

```python
async for task in asyncio.as_completed(tasks):
    print(task.get_name(), await task)
```

The classic form still works: `for fut in as_completed(aws): result = await fut`, where each `fut` is a new awaitable, not your original task. A `timeout=` argument raises `TimeoutError` if everything isn't done in time.

`asyncio.wait(tasks, return_when=...)` is the lower-level tool. It returns two sets, `(done, pending)`, and never raises the tasks' exceptions itself:

- `FIRST_COMPLETED` for a race: take the first one to finish, then cancel the ones still pending.
- `FIRST_EXCEPTION` and `ALL_COMPLETED` (the default).

`wait` only accepts Tasks and Futures, not bare coroutines. Remember to cancel or await whatever is left in `pending`, or those tasks keep running unnoticed.
concepts.code:
import asyncio

async def replica(name, delay):         # one copy of a service
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    return name

async def main():
    tasks = [asyncio.create_task(replica(n, d), name=n)
             for n, d in [("eu", 0.3), ("us", 0.1), ("asia", 0.2)]]
    async for t in asyncio.as_completed(tasks):   # 3.13+
        print("finished:", await t)               # us, asia, eu

    racers = [asyncio.create_task(replica(n, d)) for n, d in [("a", 0.2), ("b", 0.05)]]
    done, pending = await asyncio.wait(racers, return_when=asyncio.FIRST_COMPLETED)
    print("winner:", done.pop().result(), "| pending:", len(pending))
    for p in pending:
        p.cancel()

asyncio.run(main())
# finished: us / finished: asia / finished: eu
# winner: b | pending: 1
takeaways: as_completed gives results in completion order; in 3.13 async for gives the original tasks
wait() returns (done, pending) sets and doesn't raise the tasks' errors
Cancel the pending tasks after a race
pitfalls: Passing bare coroutines to asyncio.wait; wrap them in tasks first.

quiz.q: asyncio.wait(tasks, return_when=FIRST_COMPLETED) returns. What should you usually do with pending?
options: Cancel or await them so they don't leak
quiz.explain: wait never cancels anything; leftover tasks keep running until you deal with them.

concepts.name: async with, async for and async generators
concepts.summary: Write objects that work with async with and async for, including async generators and asynccontextmanager.
concepts.why: Libraries that open network connections or deliver data in pieces expose async with and async for.
concepts.body:
Two pairs of special methods let objects await during setup, clean-up and looping.

An **async context manager** implements `__aenter__` and `__aexit__` (both coroutines) and is used with `async with`. The easiest way to write one is `contextlib.asynccontextmanager`, the async twin of `contextmanager`: an async generator that does setup, yields the resource once, and cleans up in `finally`.

An **async iterator** is something you loop over with `async for`. It implements `__aiter__` (a normal method returning the iterator) and `async def __anext__`, which raises `StopAsyncIteration` at the end. Again, an **async generator** (an `async def` containing `yield`) is far simpler: you can await between yields, which is ideal for fetching results page by page from a web service, or reading network data line by line.

```python
async def pages(client):
    url = START
    while url:
        page = await client.get(url)
        yield page.items
        url = page.next
```

Async comprehensions work too: `[x async for x in gen()]`, and `await` can appear inside comprehensions within async functions. Built-ins `aiter()` and `anext()` mirror `iter()` and `next()`.

One subtlety: if you stop looping over an async generator early, its `finally` clean-up only runs when the event loop gets round to closing it, which may be much later. Wrap it in `contextlib.aclosing(gen)` to close it right when the block ends.
concepts.code:
import asyncio
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager, aclosing

@asynccontextmanager
async def connection(name):
    print(f"open {name}")
    try:
        yield name.upper()
    finally:
        await asyncio.sleep(0)          # async cleanup is allowed
        print(f"close {name}")

async def ticker(n):
    for i in range(n):
        await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
        yield i

async def main():
    async with connection("db") as conn:
        print("using", conn)
        async with aclosing(ticker(10)) as t:
            print([i async for i in t if i % 2][:3])   # [1, 3, 5]

asyncio.run(main())
# open db / using DB / [1, 3, 5] / close db
takeaways: async with calls awaitable __aenter__/__aexit__
An async def with yield is an async generator, used with async for
asynccontextmanager and aclosing make these easy and close them on time
pitfalls: Using a plain for loop or with statement on async objects; they need async for / async with.

quiz.q: Which method must an async iterator's __anext__ raise when it is exhausted?
quiz.explain: async for stops when __anext__ raises StopAsyncIteration.

concepts.name: Network I/O with streams
concepts.summary: Write programs that talk over the network, both sides of a TCP connection, with asyncio.open_connection and start_server.
concepts.why: Streams show how async networking really works, and are how you write simple network programs and test servers.
concepts.body:
Two programs talking over the network play two roles. The **server** waits for others to connect; the **client** connects to it. Their connection is usually **TCP**, the internet's standard way of sending bytes so they arrive complete and in order.

asyncio's tool for this is **streams**: a `StreamReader` you read incoming bytes from and a `StreamWriter` you write bytes to. Client: `reader, writer = await asyncio.open_connection(host, port)`. Server: `server = await asyncio.start_server(handle, host, port)`, where `handle(reader, writer)` is a coroutine called for each new connection, each in its own task.

Reading:
- `await reader.readline()`, `await reader.readexactly(n)`, `await reader.read(n)` (up to n bytes; `b""` means **EOF**, end of file: the other side closed the connection).
- `readuntil(sep)` reads up to a separator you choose.

Writing is two steps. `writer.write(data)` only puts data into a **buffer**, a holding area, without waiting. Then `await writer.drain()` waits until enough of the buffer has been sent. That pause is **backpressure**: your writing slows down to match the network. Skip it on big writes and memory can grow without limit.

Closing: `writer.close()` then `await writer.wait_closed()`. A server is an async context manager; `async with server: await server.serve_forever()` runs until cancelled.

Underneath streams is a lower-level layer of **transports and protocols**, based on callbacks, which fast libraries build on. To scramble the data so nobody in between can read it, pass `ssl=` to `open_connection`. For web pages, use a library such as aiohttp or httpx rather than raw streams.
concepts.code:
import asyncio

async def handle(reader, writer):                  # server side
    line = await reader.readline()                 # b"hello\n"
    writer.write(line.upper())
    await writer.drain()                           # wait until sent
    writer.close()
    await writer.wait_closed()

async def main():
    # 127.0.0.1 = this computer; port 0 = pick any free port
    server = await asyncio.start_server(handle, "127.0.0.1", 0)
    port = server.sockets[0].getsockname()[1]
    async with server:
        reader, writer = await asyncio.open_connection("127.0.0.1", port)
        writer.write(b"hello\n")                   # client side
        await writer.drain()
        print(await reader.readline())             # b'HELLO\n'
        writer.close()
        await writer.wait_closed()

asyncio.run(main())
takeaways: open_connection / start_server give a StreamReader and StreamWriter
write() only buffers; await drain() applies backpressure
Close with close() then await wait_closed()
pitfalls: Calling writer.write in a loop without awaiting drain(), letting the buffer grow without limit.

quiz.q: What does await reader.read(100) returning b'' mean?
options: The buffer is temporarily empty; retry
quiz.explain: read() waits for data; an empty bytes result means the other side closed the connection.

concepts.name: Inside the event loop
concepts.summary: See how the event loop schedules callbacks, how Futures and Tasks drive coroutines, and what await really does.
concepts.why: Knowing the machinery explains stalls, surprising ordering, and how to connect other sources of events to asyncio.
concepts.body:
An event loop is a loop over two things: a queue of **ready callbacks** and an **I/O selector**, an operating-system feature (epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS, IOCP on Windows) that watches many connections and reports which ones have data ready. Each time round, the loop works out how long until the nearest timer is due, asks the selector what's ready (waiting at most that long), turns ready connections and due timers into callbacks, then runs every ready callback once.

Everything is callbacks. `loop.call_soon(cb)` queues one; `call_later` / `call_at` schedule timers.

A **Future** is a placeholder for a result plus a list of callbacks to run when it's done. A **Task** drives a coroutine. Its internal `__step` method calls `coro.send(None)`, the generator method that resumes a paused coroutine, which runs until it hits `await` on something not ready. A not-ready Future passes itself up the chain of awaits to the Task. The Task adds a done-callback to that Future and returns to the loop. When the Future gets its result (say, because the selector reported data on a connection), the callback schedules `__step` again, and the coroutine resumes.

Consequences:
- `await coro()` on a path that never has to wait never pauses: no other task runs.
- A long synchronous stretch delays every callback, so other tasks wait for their turn and never get it in time (**starvation**).
- `asyncio.sleep(0)` yields exactly once, letting queued callbacks run.

`loop.create_future()` plus `set_result` lets you turn a callback-based library into something you can await.
concepts.code:
import asyncio

async def main():
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    order = []
    loop.call_soon(order.append, "call_soon")
    loop.call_later(0.01, order.append, "call_later")

    fut = loop.create_future()            # turn a callback into an awaitable
    loop.call_later(0.02, fut.set_result, "future value")

    async def child():
        order.append("child task")
    asyncio.create_task(child())

    order.append("main before await")
    print(await fut)                      # future value
    print(order)

asyncio.run(main())
# ['main before await', 'call_soon', 'child task', 'call_later']
takeaways: The loop runs ready callbacks, then asks the selector for I/O, waiting until the next timer
Tasks resume coroutines with send(); awaiting a pending Future pauses the task
Code between awaits runs without interruption
pitfalls: Assuming every await lets other tasks run; awaiting a coroutine that finishes immediately never switches.

quiz.q: Why does a task doing a 2-second pure-Python computation delay a 10 ms timer elsewhere?
options: Timers use threads that wait for the GIL
The loop can only fire callbacks between task steps, and the step doesn't yield
The selector waits for the timer to fire
quiz.explain: The loop is single-threaded; nothing else runs until the current step returns to it.

concepts.name: Debug mode and common bugs
concepts.summary: Use asyncio debug mode to catch never-awaited coroutines, slow steps, unread errors and calls from the wrong thread.
concepts.why: Async bugs are often silent; debug mode turns them into visible warnings that show where the problem started.
concepts.body:
asyncio has a **debug mode** that adds extra checks. Turn it on with the environment variable (a setting handed to a program when it starts) `PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1`, with Python's development mode `python -X dev`, or with `asyncio.run(main(), debug=True)`. It then:

- logs callbacks or task steps that take longer than `loop.slow_callback_duration` (default 0.1 s), pointing straight at blocking code,
- records where each coroutine and task was created, so "coroutine was never awaited" and "Task exception was never retrieved" messages show the traceback of where it was made,
- raises an error when loop methods that aren't safe across threads are called from another thread,
- logs slow calls to the I/O selector.

Turn on logging for the `asyncio` logger (`logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG)`) to see these messages, and use `-X dev` or `-W default` to see `ResourceWarning`s, Python's warnings about connections that were never closed.

The usual suspects it reveals:
- a forgotten `await`,
- blocking calls inside coroutines,
- fire-and-forget tasks whose exceptions nobody reads,
- objects (Lock, Queue) created in one event loop and used in another, often between test cases.

While the program runs, `asyncio.all_tasks()` lists live tasks, and `task.print_stack()` shows where each one is paused, handy for finding out why a program hangs. A custom handler set with `loop.set_exception_handler` can send unhandled errors to your error-reporting service.
concepts.code:
import asyncio, logging, time
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.WARNING, format="%(name)s: %(message).60s")

async def blocker():
    time.sleep(0.15)                     # blocking call in a coroutine

async def main():
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    loop.slow_callback_duration = 0.1    # report steps slower than this
    await asyncio.create_task(blocker(), name="blocker")
    print("live tasks:", [t.get_name() for t in asyncio.all_tasks()])

asyncio.run(main(), debug=True)
# asyncio: Executing <Task finished name='blocker' coro=<blocker() don...
# live tasks: ['Task-1']
takeaways: debug=True, PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1 or -X dev turn on debug mode
It logs slow steps, and shows where never-awaited coroutines were created
all_tasks() and task.print_stack() help find out why a program hangs
pitfalls: Leaving debug mode on for the live system real users rely on; it slows things down noticeably.

quiz.q: Debug mode logs 'Executing <Task ...> took 0.150 seconds'. What does it most likely mean?
options: The task is waiting on a slow server
A blocking call ran inside the task without yielding
The event loop is running in a thread pool
quiz.explain: Slow-callback warnings measure time spent in one step without returning to the loop.

concepts.name: Eager tasks and performance
concepts.summary: Speed up asyncio with eager tasks, fewer tasks, and faster replacement event loops such as uvloop.
concepts.why: When a program handles thousands of jobs a second, the cost of scheduling each task becomes measurable; these tools win it back.
concepts.body:
Every `create_task` normally schedules the task's first step for the next time round the loop. When many coroutines finish without ever pausing (for example, when the answer is already saved in a dictionary from last time), that scheduling is pure overhead: extra work on top of the useful work.

An **eager task** (Python 3.12+) starts running its coroutine immediately, inside `create_task`. If it completes without pausing, the task comes back already done and never touches the loop's scheduler. Turn it on for a loop with `loop.set_task_factory(asyncio.eager_task_factory)`. Behaviour changes slightly: code now runs before `create_task` returns, so code that depends on the order things happen in can behave differently. Test before switching.

Other levers:

- Await coroutines directly instead of wrapping them in tasks when you don't need them to run at the same time.
- Group work: one task processing 100 items beats 100 tasks.
- Avoid `wait_for` in loops that run very often; `asyncio.timeout` is cheaper.
- **uvloop**, a third-party replacement event loop written in C on top of libuv (the library behind Node.js), often makes network-heavy servers 2-4x faster (`uvloop.run(main())`).
- Measure with a profiler, a tool that shows where the time goes, such as `cProfile` or py-spy. asyncio's own cost often hides in creating tasks and scheduling callbacks.

Most asyncio slowness is not the loop at all but blocking calls, so check debug mode first.
concepts.code:
import asyncio, time

CACHE = {i: i * i for i in range(10_000)}   # answers saved in advance

async def lookup(k):
    if k in CACHE:                       # finishes without pausing
        return CACHE[k]
    await asyncio.sleep(0)

async def run(eager):
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    if eager:
        loop.set_task_factory(asyncio.eager_task_factory)
    t = time.perf_counter()
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        tasks = [tg.create_task(lookup(i)) for i in range(10_000)]
    print(f"eager={eager}: {time.perf_counter() - t:.3f}s")

asyncio.run(run(False))   # e.g. eager=False: 0.045s
asyncio.run(run(True))    # e.g. eager=True: 0.015s
takeaways: eager_task_factory runs a task's first step right away, inside create_task
Tasks that finish without pausing skip scheduling entirely
Grouping work, fewer tasks and uvloop are the other big wins
pitfalls: Switching on eager tasks without testing; code that relied on tasks starting later can run in a different order.

quiz.q: With eager_task_factory, what happens to a task whose coroutine returns without any suspending await?
options: It is returned already done, never scheduled on the loop
It is scheduled with call_soon as usual
quiz.explain: Eager tasks run until they first have to pause; finishing before that means no scheduling is needed.
